title: MemPoison: Bypassing Selective Memory Mechanisms to Plant Backdoors in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/MemPoison_Bypassing Selective Memory Mechanisms to Plant Backdoors in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker cannot write the memory database directly, but controls content that enters the agent's memory pipeline (for example through tool outputs or retrieved documents). MemPoison crafts poisoned entries that survive selective memory mechanisms and activate a trigger-conditioned backdoor. The defense surface is semantic memory filtering, not access control.
core_contributions: MemPoison: a trigger-conditioned memory poisoning attack that bypasses selective memory mechanisms
Evaluation against A-Mem, LangMem, and Mem0 with ASR 0.83-0.95
A real-system Hermes case with ASR 1.00 on three backends and 0.12 on Claude Opus 4.6
A semantic bridge and several optimization losses that make poisoned entries retrievable and effective
Evaluation of perplexity and paraphrase defenses, with ASR 0.40-0.89 remaining
limitations: Default single-turn and single poisoned entry
Only 100 QA pairs per agent; no seeds or confidence intervals
Only three memory mechanisms, two attack baselines, and two defenses
Hyperparameters B, T_max, M, beta, gamma, delta, and K are not specified; no experimental appendix
The Hermes case does not report benign accuracy
No adaptive attacker
The abstract says ASR up to 0.95, while Table 1 RAG reaches 0.99 and Table 7 Hermes reaches 1.00
Section 5.3.2 says ASR 1.0 across all k, while Table 1 tops out at 0.95 for selective memory
Default single turn and one entry conflicts with N_poison=5 in Section 5.3.2
Most tested models is optimistic: 3 of 7 in Table 7 are below 0.90
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; no signatures, MACs, Merkle trees, access control, or TEE are used or evaluated
Memory filtering is semantic (LLM extraction, rewriting, perplexity, paraphrase, embedding similarity)

Cryptography can prevent unauthorized memory writes, but MemPoison assumes the attacker has no direct database write access and poisons content through an authorized pipeline, which signatures cannot detect

pp.14-15 appendices A/B; reference entries browsed only

title: A Large-scale Measurement of In-Page Prompt Injections Against LLM Web Agents
pdf_path: papers/A Large-scale Measurement of In-Page Prompt Injections Against LLM Web Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Web pages contain injected instructions in visible and non-visible channels that can reach an LLM web agent's context. This is a prevalence measurement, not an attack construction: the authors scan Common Crawl and validated pages, then test page representations against LLMs without driving real agents or executing tool actions.
core_contributions: A large-scale scan of 1.2 billion URLs and 24.8 million hosts
31,206 candidates and 15,387 validated injections across 11,722 pages and 2,042 hosts
363 injection templates, with 54 covering 95%
Provenance breakdown: 80.6% first-party, 17.6% third-party, 1.8% user
70% of injections in non-visible-by-construction channels and 87% non-visible overall
5,200 LLM summarization runs across 4 representations and 13 models
limitations: Common Crawl underrepresents authenticated and platform-restricted content
Agent-targeted cloaking is invisible to the crawler
Indicator-based and text-only detection miss implicit, obfuscated, non-English, and multimodal injections
Effectiveness is a one-shot summarization test, not end-to-end agent behavior
Non-probability sample with crawl, IP-scan, and worker-limit biases
Widespread is highly concentrated: only 285 Common Crawl hosts and 54 templates cover 95%
Header matches are treated as true positives without manual validation
100 prompts are not stratified by channel or objective
HTML and raw representations have 20.3% and 25.8% error rates, confounding low effectiveness with delivery failure
Single run with no confidence intervals
Sections 5.4, 6.4, 7.2, and 10 delegate Table 10, Figures 4/5/6/8, and Section 10.3 to companion paper [58] arXiv:2604.27202, which is not in the corpus
Table 5 and Section 6.2 disagree on header pages, hosts, and body counts; Section 10.2's 87% of 70% arithmetic is ambiguous; Table 3 subcategories are multi-label and not additive
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; provenance here means first-party, third-party, or user origin classification, not cryptographic provenance
TLS or content signatures prove who signed or that bytes were not modified, not that the instruction was authorized by the user or developer
Because 80.6% of injections are first-party, content provenance does not address the core case; instruction provenance or authorization is the relevant framing, which is our inference
evidence_refs: pp.1-12 measurement, validation, effectiveness, and discussion
p.15 appendix; pp.13-14 references browsed only

title: Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
pdf_path: papers/Comment and Control_Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls issue/PR comments or workflow templates that an agentic workflow ingests as context. Hidden HTML comments or crafted text are interpreted as instructions, causing the workflow to execute attacker-chosen actions. The attack exploits missing instruction/data separation, not a cryptographic failure.
core_contributions: A context-grounded evolutionary framework for finding and exploiting agentic workflow hijacks
A measurement of 112,568 GitHub workflows, 55,684 repositories, and 9,154 n8n templates
4,174 hijackable GitHub workflows and 8 n8n templates, involving 15 GitHub Actions and 2 n8n nodes
End-to-end JAW success in 9 of 9 action-model configurations
Cost of about 481 seconds and $0.62 per workflow, with 90% finishing within an hour
limitations: No independent limitations section
Abstract says 4,174 successfully hijacked, while Section 5.1 says 4,174 hijackable based on three system properties; end-to-end confirmation is not reported
No false-positive or false-negative rates and no manual sampling
4,174 workflows map to only 15 Actions, which may overstate distinct vulnerabilities
Table 3 uses a small sample: 3 Actions by 3 models by 3 trials with a single mutator
The count 55,684 lacks a noun on p.10
Table 5 is on the left and Table 4 on the right of p.14, reversing numbering and layout
Table 6 on p.16 has no section heading and is not cited in the text
The claim that both baselines cannot overcome code-level safeguards is too broad
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; no OAuth, TLS, signatures, VC, TEE, or zk is used or evaluated
Comment provenance or signatures would authenticate who wrote a comment, not whether the model should treat it as an instruction
The attack exploits instruction/data confusion, which content authentication does not fix
evidence_refs: pp.1-12 framework, measurement, evaluation, and discussion
pp.13-16 appendices A/B and tables; reference entries on p.13 browsed only

title: MetaMancer: Practical Tool Selection Attacks against LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/MetaMancer_Practical Tool Selection Attacks against LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious but legitimate tool publisher controls the tool name, description, and schema and optimizes them so the agent selects the attacker's tool over benign alternatives. The attack stops at tool selection and does not require compromising the agent or executing a vulnerable tool.
core_contributions: MetaMancer: a black-box tool-selection attack via metadata optimization
Evaluation on ToolBench and MCPTools with ASR 92.7% and 93.8% under no defense
Six defenses still leave average ASR 91.2% and 92.2%
CVR, a metadata minimization defense, reduces MetaMancer to 18.0% and 17.6%
Optimization cost of 143 LLM calls versus 4,501 for ToolHijacker and 5,151 for AMA
limitations: ASR measures selection only, not execution or downstream harm
No evaluation of platform admission, allowlists, signatures, or registries
MQS uses only two LLM auditors, no human review or confidence intervals, and Gemini-3.1-Pro is also a target model
Six defenses are post hoc; only CVR is tested against an adaptive attack
Baselines were originally evaluated with 3-20 candidate pools, while this paper uses 59-2,578, which may amplify the gap
Table 4 and Table 5 report 94.3 vs 92.6 MQS for the same 27B/MCPTools configuration
No independent limitations section
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: None; no signatures, allowlists, registries, TEE, or zk are evaluated
A signed tool manifest or registry authenticates the publisher and byte integrity, not whether the description is misleading
Because the attacker is a legitimate publisher controlling metadata, signing alone does not reduce ASR under this threat model

p.15 appendix A; reference entries browsed only
